title: I have sinned (2 Samuel 12:13)
hook: David answers in two Hebrew words, with no excuse

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathan's story of the ewe lamb, and the line that turned it into a mirror. Your line was the judge has written his own verdict. Did you let anyone tell you something hard? Today, the king answers. Day seven hundred forty-eight.
screen: `THE JUDGE HAS WRITTEN HIS OWN VERDICT.`

segments.voice: Nathan has just finished speaking. The room is quiet. A king who has had a man killed now stands accused, in his own palace, by someone with no army behind him. There are plenty of things a king could say next. He could call the guards. He could explain the pressures of war. He could point out that Uriah died in battle, which, on paper, is true. He could ask who else knows. The text gives him none of those lines. It gives him one short answer.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.` → `A KING COULD SAY MANY THINGS.` → `HE SAYS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I have sinned against the LORD." In Hebrew it's two words, chatati l'Adonai. No because. No but. No list of reasons. It helps to hear it next to another king. Back in the first book of Samuel, Saul is confronted by the prophet Samuel after he disobeys a command. Saul also says I have sinned. And then he keeps going: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. The confession comes with a reason attached, and the reason does some of the work of an excuse. David's sentence stops where it starts. Nathan's reply comes just as fast: the Lord has put away your sin; you shall not die. That doesn't mean nothing follows. The very next words say the child born to David will die, and the chapters ahead are full of trouble in his house. Forgiveness here is real, and so are the consequences. The text holds both and doesn't flatten either. Jewish tradition has a name for this kind of turning: teshuvah, returning. And the heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this very moment, when Nathan the prophet came to David. Some readers hear that psalm as the long version of what David said here in two words. So what makes this short answer matter? Not that David feels bad. A person can feel bad and still explain. It's that he stops defending himself. He names what he did, and who it was against, and lets it stand. Some readers notice the oddness of the target: he wronged Uriah, and Bathsheba, and the people he commanded. Yet he says, against the Lord. Some hear that as the deepest admission, that every wrong to a person is also a wrong before God. The sentence is short. It is not small.
screen: `TWO WORDS IN HEBREW. NO BECAUSE.` · `SAUL SAID IT, THEN EXPLAINED.` · then, large: `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · then: `FORGIVEN, AND STILL CONSEQUENCES.` · `PSALM 51 LOOKS BACK HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one wrong without an excuse. Settle, and breathe. Let one recent thing come to mind where you got it wrong: a sharp word, a broken promise, a corner cut. Now say it to yourself in one plain sentence. I did this. Then notice the urge to add because, and let the because go. You don't need to explain it right now. Just let the sentence stand on its own. If there's someone you owe that sentence to, picture saying it to them, short, with nothing after it. If you pray, you can bring it before God the same way. The bell holds the time.
Chatati. The two Hebrew words David said to Nathan, meaning I have sinned, with no excuse attached. Today's word.
Your line: no because, no but. Today, when you apologize for anything, even something small, stop before the because. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews speak of teshuvah, returning, as naming a wrong, regretting it, and changing course; David's answer to Nathan can be read alongside Psalm 51, which its heading links to this moment.

fork.setup: you're David. a prophet has just told you, in your own palace, that you are the man. what do you say?
options: I have sinned against the Lord.
fork.reveal: David says it plainly, with no reason attached, and Nathan answers at once that his sin is put away.

original.note: Hebrew: I have sinned, David's first word to Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king feeling sorry.
what it means: David names what he did and stops defending himself; forgiveness comes, and so do consequences.
what a scholar hears: chatati l'Adonai, two words, set against Saul's I have sinned with its because in 1 Samuel 15:24.

sources.quoted: I have sinned against the LORD

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording 'I have sinned against the LORD' at 2 Samuel 12:13.
The Hebrew is חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה, two words, as the outline's hook says; please confirm. The transliteration l'Adonai follows the custom of reading the divine name as Adonai.
Saul's confession with its reason paraphrases 1 Samuel 15:24.
Psalm 51's heading (verses 1–2 in Jewish numbering) links the psalm to Nathan's coming to David.
The reading of 'against the Lord' as including every wrong to a person is attributed to 'some readers'; a Keeper may wish to name a commentator.
